public_notes.title: Homelands And Forced Land Loss
public_notes.text: The Nation's history identifies the Kanza, also called Kaw or Kansa, with the Great Plains and what is now Kansas. It describes successive treaties shrinking the homeland, followed by forced cession of Kansas lands. The people then had to purchase land in Indian Territory using proceeds from former Kansas holdings. The account connects allotment with the breakup of collective landholding and later reservoir flooding with damage to the old town of Washunga and Tribal institutions. These are the Nation's historical accounts, not a present-day map of property or jurisdiction. Related Dhegiha peoples remain distinct Nations.

public_notes.title: Rebuilding Government And Language Learning
public_notes.text: The Nation's government history describes citizens organizing constitutional work through meetings, surveys, a petition and a vote accepting a new constitution in 2011. Its pages differ on the exact date: the history places the vote in August, while the constitution page labels ratification in April. The year is supported; the day and month remain unresolved. The language page separately offers a public index of Kanza learning resources, including a basic course and online learning. Institutional changes do not mark the beginning of the people, and a resource index is not proof of fluency outcomes or permission to copy its materials.

public_notes.title: Two Peoples And Forced Relocation
public_notes.text: The Tribe's history identifies Otoe and Missouria as related but distinct peoples with a shared later history. It describes centuries of trade along the Missouri River, population losses from disease and warfare, and Missouria survivors living with Otoe relatives in the late eighteenth century. The account dates confinement on Nebraska's Big Blue River reservation to 1855 and removal to Red Rock, Oklahoma, to 1881. It also records broken promises, pressure to abandon established livelihoods and boarding-school punishment for speaking the language. Those accounts explain dispossession without reducing living people to loss; historical dates do not define the beginning of either people.

public_notes.title: Preservation And Language Led By The Tribe
public_notes.text: The Tribe's preservation page records an application in spring 2015 and National Park Service recognition of its preservation office in spring 2016. It describes review of federal projects and consultation concerning places important to the Tribe; that process is not a guarantee that a project will be stopped. A separately dated May 2026 story reports an April language-learning banquet and learning through youth programs, a local school and online classes. These are practical, community-led forms of continuity. Office recognition is not Tribal recognition, and the reported event does not certify today's course availability or language outcomes.
